Gaming_Tech.title: Zuckerberg's image is in trouble - but Meta's business is booming
Gaming_Tech.text:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.

"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."

Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.

It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.

For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.

That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.

And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.

His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".

Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.

But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.

It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?

It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.

Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.

Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.

And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.

Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.

Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.

In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.

And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.

The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.

Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.

But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.

While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.

And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.

One view popular among critics is that the company has tested consumer tolerance for bad behaviour and until now, its business has mostly managed to withstand the blowback. In other words, people will continue to use the products even if they don't like the company.

"I think they're in a remarkably good position that I didn't expect them to be in," says Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy.

However, Meta's move into AI depends partly on rebuilding public trust.

Last month, the company launched its new AI personal assistant app, Muse. Crucially, Muse is an AI agent, meaning it can carry out tasks in multiple stages and work on something over several hours (in contrast to chatbots like ChatGPT, which tend to do one task at a time).

It's the first AI agent from a major tech firm to become publicly available. A New York Times tech reporter who used the app for two weeks says he was "blown away"; the app called his dental insurer on his behalf, ordered him groceries and tracked his credit card spending in a spreadsheet.

But Muse works best when users hand over some of their most personal information to the company, including credit card information, purchase histories and access to email inboxes.

It's a big ask for a company whose reputation on privacy has been sullied, starting a decade ago with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which followed the revelation that the data of millions of Facebook users was breached and used by a political consulting firm.

Just two days after Zuckerberg's keynote at Meta Connect, another New Mexico jury found Meta lied about how Facebook used personal information. (The company has said it disagrees with the verdict and will defend itself against what it says are efforts to distort its record.)

So are customers willing to hand over that data for the convenience of using Muse?

Some users say yes. Since its launch one month ago, Muse already has more than five million downloads and more than three million weekly active users - outpacing the adoption of ChatGPT when that was first introduced, in the North American market.

Zuckerberg has laid out a vision in which Muse couples with an ever-expanding line-up of Meta AI smart glasses, enabling users to summon hands-free what he calls "personal superintelligence".

Meta clearly has big plans for its smart glasses. "I think they're making an investment to position themselves as a category leader," says Kate Winick, principal analyst at Forrester, covering social media and influencers. "However big this category turns out to be, they will own it - for now."

The glasses are divisive, and have been labelled by some as "pervert glasses" because they can be used to film covertly. The company has moved to stop users from tampering with the light that indicates a photo or video is being captured. Zuckerberg also just announced new audio-only smart glasses, an apparent bid to quell privacy concerns.

But the company's most strident critics remain wary.

"Consumers know that Meta has problems, and that to date we haven't been able to trust them to make their products safe for children. So why would a consumer want to trust them with some of their most private and sensitive information?" says Brooke Istook of the Heat Initiative, a campaign group.

In the end, the bulk of users may be willing to make some concessions on privacy if it means convenience and utility, says Moorhead. "If the consumer sees the trade-off as beneficial, then they'll keep it going," he says. "This is why Facebook and Instagram still have billions of users."

On the financial front, the social media advertising business – its cash cow – routinely brings in significant revenue. Meta reported $60.8bn in revenue and $15.9bn in profit for the second quarter of this year.

Consistent profits have helped fuel bets from the much-mocked Metaverse, to its current mass expansion of AI infrastructure.

And on Muse? "It's a very real time-saving benefit that a lot of people will want and will like," says Winick.

AI investment is not cheap. Meta has now taken on $83.7bn in long-term debt, according to its most recent financial statement.

Still, Meta executives are bullish about the company's pivot to AI. "It's really about your agent, who can do work on your behalf, who is your constant ally in whatever you're trying to accomplish in your goals in your life," Andrew Bosworth, the company's chief technology officer, said in an interview with the BBC.

Meta has big plans. But its future may ultimately depend on whether its users can trust it.

Gaming_Tech.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
Gaming_Tech.text:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.

Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.

The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.

It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.

Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".

The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.

The BBC has approached him for comment.

A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.

Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.

University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".

"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.

Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".

"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'
Gaming_Tech.text:
Warning: This article contains strong language.

Meredith Whittaker has little patience for the AI doom that dominates headlines - she thinks warnings of AI turning on humanity is a fear "not anchored in science".

"The risk is very real," says the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app of the same name, "but it's not the shiny ghost stories the wild-eyed boys are talking about".

Instead, she believes the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly.

She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material, reportedly leading the US to prepare a military response.

"We almost went to war with China," she tells BBC Global Women.

"A system that produces faulty intelligence and almost gets us into a war with China should not be considered super-intelligent by any standards."

Signal has an estimated 40-70 million users - a drop in the ocean next to WhatsApp, which has billions.

But it is renowned for its tough stance on protecting users' privacy - it hides who is sending a message from its own servers, limiting the data available to outside observers or hackers.

Time magazine named Whittaker one of the most powerful people in AI. She moves through the rooms where its future is discussed, from Silicon Valley boardrooms to Downing Street, Davos and the Vatican.

She studied literature at university and joined Google in 2006 as an entry-level temp with no computer science degree.

In late 2017, she made her name when a colleague told her about Project Maven, a secret Google contract with the US Department of Defense to build AI for drone targeting.

She understood what it meant to "compress the kill chain": to shrink the time between a machine flagging a target and someone deciding to fire, reducing deliberation. With thousands of colleagues, she pushed back.

"This is going to launder bad intelligence and bad data," she remembers arguing publicly.

The following year Whittaker helped organise a walkout, in which some 20,000 staff protested against the company's handling of several issues, including what they felt was the rushed introduction of new technology. Google dropped the contract and Palantir picked it up.

She draws a direct line from Maven to the US missile attack on a school in Iran this year, which she says relied on the system and on outdated intelligence that identified the school as a military target.

"This is exactly what we were warning about in 2017," she says.

In response, Palantir told Global Women there was "no evidence that Palantir's software was at fault in this terrible tragedy".

It added that "Palantir is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies". And earlier this year it's UK and Europe boss, Louis Mosley told the BBC that "there's always a human in the loop, so there is always a human that makes the ultimate decision".

The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".

Governments, including the UK's, argue for more access to conversations on messaging apps. They say this is to protect women and children.

At London Tech Week 2026, then Prime Minister Keir Starmer said technology companies would be expected to detect and block nude images on children's devices, or face legislation.

Whittaker argues children would be able to circumvent any such measures, calling the government's approach "an unprecedented regime of communication and information controls".

The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology told the BBC it is preparing legislation.

Would Signal leave any country, the UK included, that forced it to weaken its encryption?

"Yes! My God, I have a backbone," she says. "It doesn't change based on mood. It doesn't change based on consultants."

Faced with exposing people "who rely on us, sometimes in the context of life or death, to surveillance that could be weaponised against them", she says, "we would leave the market".

The app is fully or partially blocked in Russia, China and Iran.

Rani Govender, Head of Child Safety Online at the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, told the BBC it hears from children who have been groomed and moved on to end-to-end encrypted platforms, where they are coerced into creating child sexual abuse material.

"Tech companies are responsible for the design choices they make, and they cannot ignore the risks those choices can create for children."

But Signal does have support from some women's groups, often those from the Global South who use the app themselves.

"In a time of state surveillance and cyber-attacks, Signal is a tool for survival," says Hera Hussain, founder of the gender abuse charity Chayn, which is active throughout South Asia.

"With any platform, it can be used by bad actors too, and we have to hold that truth too."

I put to Whittaker a case from Canada, where police officers shared racist and misogynistic messages in a Signal group which leaked only when one of them passed it on to the media.

A lawyer for one officer said the men believed Signal was as private and safe as their own home.

"If they had that conversation in the kitchen and their bro snitched, would it be: 'What are we doing about kitchens?'" she asks.

"It has to work for everyone or it works for no-one. This is the principle of fundamental rights. They apply even to assholes."

She points to a US woman jailed after Meta handed over messages showing she helped her daughter access abortion in a state where it had been criminalised.

Private communication, she says, protects people from many kinds of harm - "an abusive spouse, a misogynist law enforcement officer with access to a database, or an authoritarian government that doesn't think women should get educated".

What would she want to say to a woman who wants to enter the tech field but is intimidated by the gendered aspect of the profession?

"Do you love it?" she says.

"Do you sit down at a terminal and feel a rush of energy? Do you enjoy playing with and defining AI systems?"

Then she pauses and says: "Are you able to navigate interesting and gnarly environments where not everyone is going to be chill? Because there's nothing more dangerous than being a coward in front of a bully."

I ask her if these environments are full of bullies.

Her colleague says, "I think that's 2pm" - the time we agreed to end the interview.

Meredith smiles. "I'd say don't be a simp," she says, using a term for someone who shows extreme deference to authority figures.

"It's not going to help you. Don't laugh at the joke if you don't think it's funny."

Additional reporting by Katie Roberts

Gaming_Tech.title: Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.

She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.

For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.

This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.

For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs, external. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes, external.

Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.

Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.

For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.

Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019.

In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.

Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".

Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.

The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."

Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.

She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.

"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.

But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."

Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.

Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.

Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.

Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."

Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.

Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.

While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".

But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.

"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.

While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.

One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.

This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.

This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.

In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.

Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."

Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.

What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.

Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".

Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.

She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."

Gaming_Tech.title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
Gaming_Tech.text:
Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.

One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.

The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know.

"What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.

With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".

The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".

With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.

In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".

Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.

The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.

Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.

Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.

But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.

"Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio.

"Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."

Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".

"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

Gaming_Tech.title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
Gaming_Tech.text:
Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.

The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings.

Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia.

Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.

The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be published at the end of October.

Some of South Korea's biggest companies release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports.

These forecasts are treated with much more credibility than estimates by external analysts as they are backed by internal company data.

There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology.

The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung, with its stock market valuation crossing $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year.

Investment in the industry has surged, with US tech giants including Google, Amazon and Meta pledging to pour more than $650bn into AI projects this year.

In June, South Korea unveiled plans for at least $880bn in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to build out the country's chip manufacturing capabilities in the coming years.

Rival Asian firms in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in chip plants as demand for AI soars.

A chip shortage driven by surging demand has led firms including Samsung to raise prices, making products such as smartphones and computers more expensive.

Gaming_Tech.title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
Gaming_Tech.text:
Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar.

From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme.

It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them.

It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time, which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross".

There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom.

Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96.

The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK.

Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones.

Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable.

"At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices.

"There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe."

She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time.

Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date.

"Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said.

The Petrol Retailers Association, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying.

Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year.

Entertainment.title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Being a Traitor must be a nightmare.

While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.

Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.

And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).

When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.

Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players

Celebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses

Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?

"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."

Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."

Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."

On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised.

"I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.

"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.

"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."

I guess now we'll never know.

Back at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions.

The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy of the group by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four.

The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry, found questions being asked of her too as the day rolled on.

"I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment."

Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart is one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's confusing shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before.

Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed to be a little too trustworthy to be true.

Friday's mission raised more money for charity and also raised spirits, but not in a good way.

It involved the group paying a visit to a graveside haunted cabin to converse with the dead about matters unresolved.

"It's creepy, it's giving murder," noted Barbie actress Sharon Rooney on arrival.

Comedian Romesh Ranganathan joked that his mum was going to "absolutely hate this", as the the group gathered in a graveside chant led by the booming voice of big dog actor Michael Sheen.

The spooky task made Ranganathan himself let out a hellish scream and saw Hart come face-to face with a masked hooded creature, before team-player Croft volunteered to go head-first into a stinky old toilet in scenes resembling ITV's I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

"Guys, it's a little bit of poo," noted hardman Ross Kemp, as all around him gagged. "It's not gonna kill you."

Croft received a protective shield for his troubles, at least. "If I'd have put my hands and head down a toilet for nothing, I would've been fuming," he fairly noted.

Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday

The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked

The group, with a little help from the undead, had to find a child's toys and a woman's wedding dress and shoes. This later prompted model Jerry Hall to reminisce about her own wedding to Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

"Before I got married to Mick - we'd already been together seven years, had two children - I put on a wedding dress every day until he agreed that we get married," she revealed.

Some rancid wine that tasted like "salty bin juice", according to comedian Joanne McNally, topped off possibly the most revolting task yet.

On the way back to the castle, YouTuber King Kenny raised more suspicions about Fry having allowed him to grab a shield. "She held off to make herself look a bit innocent," he told his fellow faithfuls.

Traitor Jama smartly deflected attention away from herself by latching on to the growing suspicions around Hesmondhalgh.

Ahead of the roundtable, Fry told producers she knew she would have to fight like her life depended on it - because it did - and try to disguise herself as still being a faithful.

Once discussions were under way, she played the sympathy card, claiming she had been left feeling "vulnerable" as she knew her reputation as a brain box would make her a target.

Miss Marple aka Hart wasn't going to let her off the hook that easily, however, noting how Fry's argument the previous night had contradicted that of the innocent but now sadly now departed Myha'la.

In a nice moment of levity in another tense debate, comedian Joe Lycett reminded the traitors - and pointedly, Hesmondhalgh - that he would "like to be recruited at some stage". He stressed: "I'm still very much available."

Hesmondhalgh laughed about how "going all dry mouthed" while defending herself was not helping her cause.

"It would be a cruel move taking the most trusted member of our group," noted Sheen.

"Cruel but clever," added Hart.

Ranganathan offered: "The person that we nominated as our most trustworthy person, we have now completely flipped on."

The traitors opted to stay out of the game themselves, before settling on Kemp, Ranganathan, his comic pal Rob Beckett and Little Mix and solo singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock.

"I think this is gonna mess with everybody's heads," said Fry.

Presenter Claudia Winkleman greeted the four of them outside the castle in the dead of night.

"Have we won?", quipped Ranganathan.

"If only it was that easy Romesh," replied the host, explaining how when they go down to the woods tonight they'll be in for a big surprise: one of them will be killed face-to-face.

Only Pinnock, it was decided, will be immune from murder in the game within a game, though the Traitors aren't to know that.

This much terror and mischief and it's not Halloween for weeks yet.

Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

Entertainment.title: Alison Hammond: 'I thought I was having heart attack on air'
Entertainment.text:
Alison Hammond has said she feared she was having a heart attack on air when she had to rush off ITV's This Morning midway through the programme last week.

The presenter appeared to clutch her chest as she left the show last Friday, and was taken to hospital to have a heart check-up.

She turned out to have suffered a panic attack, and said the experience was "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through".

Returning for her weekly slot on Friday, she told viewers: "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack. I'm so glad I'm here. I feel so grateful. I feel so thankful to God, to everything in life."

She added: "It felt like a heart attack. It was very real."

Alongside co-host Dermot O'Leary, Hammond introduced the programme by thanking him for holding the fort after her dramatic early exit, and also thanking everyone who sent good wishes.

She added: "It was the first time I've ever experienced anything like that. Secondly it was live on TV so I thought, oh my gosh, my son might be watching.

"So I just ran. I ran off TV. I would never do that normally but I just couldn't catch my breath."

The panic attack came on very quickly, she explained.

"It just was like a wave, something which I've now found out is adrenaline. That came into my body. I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack."

The experience has given her a new perspective on life, she continued.

"I'm so happy that I'm here, and I'm so happy to see you," she said, putting both hands on Dermot's cheeks before hugging him.

"You were absolutely wonderful. And I'm so glad we're alive, and if anything it's made me look at life so much differently. Taking stock, look after my health. I'm drinking a lot of water."

The 51-year-old compared the feeling of the panic attack to crossing into a "surreal" place like the otherworldly Upside Down in TV show Stranger Things.

"I felt like I went into the other world - what's that show that I loved? Stranger Things. You know when you go into the Upside Down world? I felt like I went into the Upside Down world.

"I couldn't grasp my breath, and it was a panic attack."

Hammond and O'Leary also spoke further about panic attacks with former BBC Breakfast host and psychologist Dr Sian Williams, who has written a book about anxiety.

Hammond said she had been unsure about returning to This Morning - but felt that if she didn't come back this week, she may never do so.

"I'll be honest with you, I was anxious about coming back. But I thought, if I don't come back today, I probably wouldn't come back... because then I would have made a thing that it's This Morning that's causing the panic.

"But it can happen anywhere. It comes in ebbs and flows."

She and Williams also discussed the pressure of presenting live TV. "I do live TV all the time, I didn't realise it was having - I don't know if it was having an impact - the fact that you have to be 'on' in order to do it. I don't know," Hammond said.

She concluded the segment by telling viewers: "I'm back, babes. Keep rolling."

Also known as anxiety attacks, panic attacks can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or whether they have a history of anxiety.

Speaking on This Morning, Dr Williams described panic attacks as "anxiety on overdrive, when you can't find the reason".

They affect more women than men and can last between five and 20 minutes, she said. People experiencing one can "ground yourself" by focusing on the moment and the safety of their surroundings, and by steadying their breathing, she added.

"A heart attack and a panic attack are different, but they can feel the same because there are similar symptoms - choking or tingling or pain in the chest.

"If it's a heart attack it tends to radiate, so if might go down your arm or into your jaw. A heart attack doesn't subside with breathing or grounding in the same way."

According to the MIND mental health charity, panic attacks are an extreme anxiety response. They can develop quickly, and come with very intense symptoms.

These are both physical and mental and the NHS's extensive list of symptoms, external includes:

Shortness of breath

Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors episode three: Emotions run high as two players banished
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.

Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.

His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table.

"Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."

There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"

Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"

But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.

Julie Hesmondhalgh noticed Myha'la ostentatiously winking at Grant before she voted for him, which later prompted the former Coronation Street actress to make one of the most impassioned - but mistaken - speeches of the night.

"It was traitor-on-traitor," she declared (it wasn't). "I don't know if anybody else saw it," (we did). "I am so excited because I truly believe we can get two in a row," (don't count on it).

The remaining traitors, Maya Jama and James Acaster, met in the turret later with the choice of murdering previously shortlisted players Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry, or seducing a third traitor to replace Grant.

The pair ultimately decided to recruit mathematician Fry, who had the most wonderful and meme-able reaction when she found out that, not only was she not being murdered, she was being seduced.

Accepting the offer, Fry joined Jama and Acaster in the turret, exclaiming as she learned their identities: "I had both of you down as faithful!"

The new trio discussed how they would approach breakfast the next morning, before Acaster delivered the line of the episode.

"It's changing a lot, this Traitors," he observed of the fluid line-up. "It's like the Sugababes."

The next morning, there were shocked faces when the players realised everybody had made it to breakfast unscathed, with the celebrities concluding that one player must have been recruited.

"It was fascinating seeing Jerry and Hannah come back," said Miranda Hart. "Hannah seemed different, as if something new has happened to her." Oh yes? "I definitely clocked a nervousness in her, which is very interesting."

We could have a first-rate traitor hunter on our hands here. But would any of Hart's fellow players feel the same way? "Poor Hannah," said McNally, "she's been recruited." Uh-oh.

As the theories continued to float around across various sub-meetings, with Hesmondhalgh, Bella Ramsey and several others setting their sights on Myha'la, the celebrities headed out to the next mission.

Presenter Claudia Winkleman explained the latest task would see them use a battering ram to break down the doors of four crypts, where they could find money to add to the prize pot - and also potentially bag some shields.

James Blunt immediately took control, assigning players various roles. "He was full army officer," Hart observed. "I found it mildly erotic."

"I don't think I've ever used a battering ram," Joe Lycett reflected. "I would use a battering ram to get into [Wicked star] Jonathan Bailey's house, but that's it."

Myha'la and Fry entered one crypt, found a shield and debated who should keep it. They agreed on Myha'la, partly because she had grabbed it first, although she sweetly suggested that the pair could keep it secret from the other players to protect both of them.

Jama and Sharon Rooney, meanwhile, scored two further shields, but the players then found that some shields would have to be given up anyway in order to unlock the final chest of prize money.

Rooney and Myha'la surrendered theirs, but traitor Jama quietly held on to hers. The other players didn't know she had one, and the TV presenter asked Rooney to keep it secret. That decision could come back to bite her in later episodes.

In the cars on the way back, the players continued to debate various hunches, with one particularly awkward journey where Myha'la and Hesmondhalgh admitted they were suspicious of each other.

"I feel like you've been a little bit vague," said Hesmondhalgh. "That's only because I've thought it's been you from day one," Myha'la replied.

We've certainly come a long way from the pair's first exchange just two episodes ago. "It's lovely to meet you Myha'la, I'm such a big fan!" - "Oh my God, thank you!"

Back in the castle, Rob Beckett had adopted a new policy. "When someone comes up to talk to me, I just agree with them, whatever they say," he laughed in the castle's diary room.

As the players gathered for the second banishment of the episode, discussion inevitably turned to prime suspect Myha'la.

"I've heard my name a whole bunch today," she acknowledged, as the others struggled to square her behaviour during the mission.

The actress became visibly emotional as she recounted the events of the crypt and attempted to justify grabbing the shield before offering it to Fry.

"I was going to give it to her," Myha'la said tearfully. "I was worried about my protection, but I thought maybe [Fry] had more heat."

Sensing that the tide was turning against Myha'la, Fry stuck the knife in. "Why would you scrabble for the shield, and then be keen to give it away?" she asked.

Despite a sprinkling of votes for other players, Myha'la became the second casualty of the episode. "I have loved getting to know you all," she said as she confirmed her faithful status to the other players.

Hart became even more suspicious of Fry, however, after realising the mathematician had orchestrated events to make Myha'la's behaviour at the crypt look less innocent. "Miss Marple is so on," Hart said with a smile.

Later, the traitors met in the turret and debated who their next victim should be, settling on a shortlist of Blunt, Ramsey and Sebastian Croft.

Acaster had a characteristically unique reason for suggesting James Blunt.

"It would make my life easier," he said, "because every time someone says 'James', I'm turning around, and half the time, it's for him."

Entertainment.title: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'
Entertainment.text:
It has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com, external.

And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release.

Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction.

"No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said.

"But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking."

The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village.

Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker.

Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before.

As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture.

And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women.

Wicker has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor.

The film has had mixed reviews from critics, with the Telegraph giving it just one star, external and calling it "a mortifying adult fairy tale", but the Times awarded four stars, external, mainly for Colman's "astonishing performance".

But since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz from audiences online - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes.

Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”.

When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for.

"And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?"

She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it.

"You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said.

Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet.

"I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see."

But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says.

He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot.

"We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said.

"But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great."

Entertainment.title: Crazy Rich Asians TV show to reunite Constance Wu and Henry Golding
Entertainment.text:
Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name.

The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor.

"It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.

The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its £110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance.

Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.

It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.

Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.

Entertainment.title: Two paintings stolen from Renoir Museum in France are recovered
Entertainment.text:
Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.

The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.

The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.

Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.

The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.

The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled

"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.

The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference.

The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.

Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.

Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August.

France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.

Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours.

They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.

The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

Entertainment.title: Luke Evans says filming new TV drama close to home was 'joyous'
Entertainment.text:
Hollywood actor Luke Evans said filming just 25 minutes from his childhood home was "joyous" - and some family members even made a cameo in the final episode of his new drama.

The Pontypool-born star, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, The Party, came up with the idea to adapt the acclaimed novel by Elizabeth Day into a drama for the screen.

For the first time in 30 years, Evans was able to film close to Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, where he grew up, as the drama was shot in Cardiff and Bridgend.

The star of Beauty and the Beast, Immortals and The Hobbit had been used to being far from home while working on the stage and films.

In The Party, Evans, 47, stars as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen.

Speaking on BBC's The One Show, he said that he had "shot in Wales" previously - when filming The Pembrokeshire Murders - but "never that close" to his family.

"Pembrokeshire is miles away from where my family are in the valleys," he said.

"They were only 25 minutes from me up the road [this time]."

He joked: "They were there all the time."

His parents Yvonne and David Evans still live in the same "narrow" terrace house he grew up in IN Aberbargoed in the Rhymney Valley.

He added: "We were having dinners on the weekend, walking the dog, enjoyed a rainy three, four months in Wales over the winter period.

"It was joyous. I loved it."

Some family members even managed to get a short cameo in the final episode of the upcoming drama.

Evans said: "[My cousins] were like 'can we be in the show?'

"They are, they're in it. My cousin and his wife and their kids are in the final episode."

After filming wrapped up, Evans headed back to New York where he starred as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway revival of The Rocky Horror Show.

"I did the show for seven months and I was coming to the end of the run - I had such an incredible experience doing the show," he said.

"It was just the most wonderful, inclusive, joyous two hours of my day. It was wonderful. The audience were just loving it."

Evans said that actor Tim Curry had been a part of his "whole journey", and that he would have people on the stage door and messages "comparing me" to him, and "how proud he would be of the performance."

Curry, who died in August, aged 80, first played the role on stage before the film version, which was released in 1975 and has remained a cult favourite.

Evans added: "So I had to send him a letter, even if he'll never read it.

"I just felt like I had to say thank you because I really believe that if it wasn't for Tim's performances as Frank-N-Furter, I don't think that film would still be around.

"He really kept that show, and the messages throughout the show are so prevalent and strong and important today as they were 53 years ago."

He received a response from Curry's team three weeks before his final performance, saying that he was "very appreciative" of that letter and thanked him for sending it.

"Sadly he passed the day after I finished," Evans said.

Earlier this summer, Evans also got the honour of switching on the Empire State Building lights for pride in New York, in the US, adding: "It was a really special thing to be asked to do."

Evans previously said that he knows "several actors" in Hollywood who have chosen not to be open about their sexuality.

He came out as gay early in his career and admitted it "wasn't easy" being one of the few out stars for a long time.

Speaking about actors who choose to not reveal their sexuality, Evans said you "never know what a person has gone through".

Asked if he thought a gay actor would ever be cast as James Bond, Evans said he was "on the list for Bond for a good decade."

He takes this as a sign that it would not be a problem but that he is "too old" for the part now.

Evans began his career as a theatre actor and later appeared in films including Clash Of The Titans (2010) and the Fast & Furious franchise.

He will play the lead role in the upcoming ITV drama The Party premiering on 11 October.

Entertainment.title: Cyberpunk 2077 movie adaptation from Paramount on the way
Entertainment.text:
A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures.

The Hollywood studio is working with producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura, known for his work on the Transformers films, and CD Projekt Red (CDPR), the developer of the sci-fi role-playing game.

CDPR's joint-chief executive Michał Nowakowski said in a statement, external the company was "excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise".

Details of the film's story, potential release date and casting information are yet to be revealed.

Despite a troubled launch in 2020, the Cyberpunk 2077 video game, which stars Keanu Reeves, has sold more than 40 million copies worldwide.

The John Wick star plays rockstar Johnny Silverhand, a terrorist whose consciousness is stored on a chip inside the body of main character V.

Set in Night City, a fictional metropolis in a dystopian version of California, players work to uncover a conspiracy involving the shady Arasaka megacorporation.

An expansion, Phantom Liberty, starring Idris Elba was released in 2023 and has sold more than 15 million copies, according to CDPR.

Cyberpunk has already been successfully adapted into a popular animated series - Edgerunners - with a second season due to premiere on Netflix later this month.

The streamer also produced The Witcher, an adaptation of CDPR's massively popular fantasy role-playing series.

Entertainment.title: Nana Patekar: Outspoken Indian actor Nana Patekar dies suddenly at 75
Entertainment.text:
Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense, fiery performances on stage and in film, has died at the age of 75 in Goa.

One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing difficult and often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.

He was admitted to a hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.

"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency. Tributes have poured in from actors and politicians across India.

Dr Salkar later told PTI news agency that the hospital team found Patekar at his home "unconscious and almost unresponsive".

The team continued giving him CPR even while taking him to the hospital, located about 10 minutes away, but he was dead by the time they reached there, he added.

Dr Salkar said Patekar had suffered a cardiac arrest, but it was not clear what had triggered it.

Family, friends and fans paid their last respects to the actor at Goa Medical College, ahead of his funeral which was to take place later in the day with full state honours at his farm house in the western city of Pune in Maharashtra state.

In the evening, his remains were flown to Pune by air ambulance, where the state's chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis paid his last respects, before Patekar's body was taken to his farm in Donje village where last rites were performed and he was cremated.

Times of India reports that his son, Malhar, told reporters afterwards that his father has not truly gone anywhere and will to remain with them - even if not physically - and his commitment to social welfare would live on.

Earlier, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality.

Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world".

Bollywood veteran Anupam Kher paid tribute to his friend on social media, saying he would miss his warmth and extraordinary performances and called him "one of the finest actors and human beings in Indian cinema".

Another Bollywood star Shah Rukh Khan called him "a mentor, a teacher, a critic and a friend", adding that Patekar has "left a void not only in the world of cinema but in the hearts of all Indians and the world".

Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention.

Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. He won his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award as well for his portrayal of the gangster Anna in the film.

He didn't look back after this and portrayed many memorable roles in films in the 1990s. The range of characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery of his craft.

Famous dialogues from his films, delivered in his inimitable rasping voice, were quoted in school corridors and tea stalls. Many professional comedians imitate his distinctive style even today.

"He had a distinctive style of working and how he approached characters. As a person, he was outspoken and difficult to get along with but directors would still want to work with him because he was simply a fantastic actor," film trade analyst Komal Nahta told BBC.

His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. His other characters, including the patriotic hero of Tirangaa and Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, also won him accolades.

Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.

Entertainment.title: Anne Carson: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet wins Nobel Prize in Literature
Entertainment.text:
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.

Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.

The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".

Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.

The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).

Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement.

"She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said.

"She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson lives in Michigan and has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022.

Anders Olsson, chairman of the Swedish Academy's Nobel committee for Literature, praised the way Carson has "broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature".

"This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms," he said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Carson's win was "an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada".

The writer's works feature "wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own," Carney wrote on social media.

"She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature."

Entertainment.title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
Entertainment.text:
The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours.

The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings.

Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts.

The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI.

Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today.

Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together".

"By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement.

"That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations."

He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future."

Last month, director general Matt Brittin said the BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services.

Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".

In June, the BBC announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage in its plan to save £500m across the corporation over the next two years.

Staff were told of proposals including ending Radio 4's The World Tonight, and reducing the number of permanent presenters on Today from five to four, with a single anchor on Saturdays.

It was revealed that BBC One's Breakfast would no longer be shown on Sunday mornings, and that the production teams making Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg and Newsnight would merge.

It followed April's announcement that the BBC would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - or almost one in 10 - in an attempt to tackle "significant financial pressures".

Last week, an influential group of MPs said the BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV, and that the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent.

In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust.

Entertainment.title: The Music Man Project fulfils late MP Sir David Amess's dream
Entertainment.text:
A music group with learning disabilities received a standing ovation as they fulfilled a dream of the late MP Sir David Amess.

The Music Man Project is a charity based in Southend-on-Sea, Essex, that teaches children and adults with learning disabilities to sing, sign and play original music.

They have performed for the King, at the Royal Albert Hall and London Palladium, but a trip to perform in New York was the dream of their former president and Southend West MP Sir David before he was murdered in 2021.

The project's founder David Stanley said: "Following his death, I just made it my mission to fulfil that promise, really, in his memory."

"So that we remember Sir David for all of the work he did for championing people with learning disabilities in Southend, and then obviously across the country, through the Music Man Project's expansion."

Stanley, who wrote, produced and featured in the show, paid a tribute to Sir David during the performance.

With a crack in his voice, he spoke into a megaphone – one of Sir David's signature accessories on the political campaign trail – the words: "We promised we'd get them to the Broadway and we did it my friend, we did it."

They performed at the Town Hall in New York with a full house of almost 1,500 people, and a venue known for its historic significance.

It was founded in 1921 by suffragists and one of the only venues in New York to openly welcome Black artists.

Stanley said his group were "perfect" and "incredible" on the night.

He said it proved what he has always said about people with learning difficulties.

"We give them the opportunities and you believe in them and you have high expectations of what they can achieve, then they will always come through, they surprise you.

"Decades ago we would have hidden certain parts of society away, now they're performing on Broadway."
